Antwerp Polyglot
ant'werp pol'ē-glot
n. (the Antwerp Polyglot, 1568–1573, the Biblia Regia printed by Christopher Plantin)
Dutch Antwerpen, a city of Brabant; Greek polyglottos, many-tongued, from polys, many, and glossa, a tongue.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Antwerp Polyglot, called the Royal Bible because Philip II paid for it, is eight folio volumes printed by Christopher Plantin between 1568 and 1573 under the editorship of Benito Arias Montano. It sets out the Hebrew, the Greek, the Vulgate, the Septuagint in Latin, the Aramaic Targums with Latin versions, and for the New Testament the Syriac, with grammars and dictionaries of the biblical languages filling the last volumes. It is the largest scholarly undertaking of the sixteenth century and it was done in a city then being torn apart by the Dutch revolt. Its politics were tangled: Montano was accused at Rome of favouring the Hebrew text above the Vulgate and had to defend himself, and Protestant scholars used the volumes freely while the crown that financed them was executing Protestants in the same provinces. That is the recurring shape of the century. The apparatus of biblical scholarship was built across the confessional line by men who would not have shared a table. “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines polyglot as having or containing many languages, and folio as a book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet of paper.

expand to see more

POL'YGLOT, a. Having or containing many languages; as a polyglot Bible or lexicon.

FO'LIO, n. A book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet of paper.

TAR'GUM, n. A translation or paraphrase of the sacred scriptures in the Chaldee language.

SYR'IAC, n. The language of Syria, especially the ancient language of that country.

Key Scripture

2Ti 2:15 — "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."

Act 2:6 — "Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language."

Act 2:11 — "Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God."

Rev 5:9 — "And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation;"

Modern Corruption

Eight folio volumes of the biblical languages, printed under a crown then executing Protestants.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a simple failure of historical honesty in both directions. Protestant accounts have sometimes written the Antwerp volumes out of the story because of who paid for them; Roman accounts have sometimes presented Montano's labours as a vindication of the Vulgate, which the volumes themselves refute by setting the Hebrew beside it and letting a reader compare.

The principle to recover is that God's intention from Pentecost forward has been a word carried in every tongue, and a polyglot is that intention in print. At Pentecost the astonishment was linguistic: “every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6), and what they heard was not a translation of a message but “the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11) in their own speech. The end of it is sung in Revelation, where the redeemed are gathered “out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation” (Rev 5:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dialektos (G1258), a language, a dialect; glossa (G1100), a tongue, a language.

Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue, a language; Acts 2:11.

Usage

"“every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6) — eight folios, 1568–1573."

"“we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11) — Hebrew, Greek, Syriac, Aramaic."

"“out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation” (Rev 5:9) — the end a polyglot serves."
